short: How far a poll's number could be from the true number just because the poll talked to a sample of people instead of everyone. A ±3 point margin on 50% means the real number is probably between 47% and 53%.

term: Margin of error on the lead
short: The gap between two candidates is less certain than either candidate's number alone, roughly twice the poll's stated margin of error. That's why a 4-point lead in a ±3 poll can still be a toss-up.
People the pollster thinks will actually vote, based on questions like past voting and interest. Each pollster decides this differently.
Everyone registered to vote, whether or not they're likely to show up.
All adults, including people who aren't registered to vote. The least precise group for predicting an election.
How many people answered the poll. More people means a smaller margin of error, but only if they were picked well.
Adjusting poll answers so the group of people who answered matches the population (for example, by age, race, education or past vote). Every pollster weights differently.
When one pollster's results lean in the same direction compared with other polls, again and again. It doesn't mean the pollster is wrong, just consistently different.
When pollsters adjust or hold back results so they look like other polls. It can make polls look more certain than they are.
A poll paid for by a campaign, a party, or a group that supports one side. It can still be accurate, but sponsors can choose which results to release.
Combining several polls into one number, which usually beats any single poll. Our formula is published on the Show Our Work page.
An expert forecaster's call on how competitive a race is, from Solid (not competitive) to Likely, Lean and Toss-up (anyone's race).
A race either side could realistically win. On our poll charts, it also means the margin-of-error range includes a tie.
The person who currently holds the seat.
The Federal Election Commission, the government agency that collects fundraising and spending reports from federal candidates.
How much money a campaign had in the bank at the end of its latest report.
Donations from people who gave $200 or less in total this cycle. Campaigns don't have to report these donors' names, so we can't see where they live.
Political action committee: a group that collects money and gives it to candidates, with legal limits on how much.
A group that can raise and spend unlimited money to support or oppose candidates, but isn't allowed to coordinate with campaigns.
Money spent by groups other than the campaign itself (like super PACs) to help or hurt a candidate.
A ballot kept separate until election officials confirm you're eligible. It counts once they do.
A ballot mailed to you so you don't have to vote in person. In Virginia anyone registered can ask for one, no reason needed.
Redrawing the lines of voting districts, usually every 10 years after the census. Where the lines go can change which party is favored.
An outside expert a court appoints to do a specific job, like drawing a district map.

FiveThirtyEight's score for how accurate and open a pollster has been in past elections, from 0 to 3 (3 is best). Their ratings were last updated in September 2024, so newer pollsters may not have one.
How far the final polls were from the actual result, and in which direction. If polls showed a Democrat up 5 and they won by 1, polls overstated Democrats by 4 points.
